904.title: A useless slaughter (1917)
904.hook: Benedict XV calls the Great War a useless slaughter and proposes peace
904.howItsDone: Catholics pray for peace and for those at war in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and later popes have also appealed for peace; some parishes remember Benedict XV's peace note when they mark the anniversary of the First World War.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fatima, and children praying the rosary in a jail cell. Your line was pray for peace. Today, a pope who tried to stop a war.

Across Europe, men are living in trenches, and whole villages have been emptied. From the Vatican, a letter goes out, addressed to the leaders of the nations at war. Catholic soldiers fight on both sides, praying to the same God in the same Mass, on opposite sides of the wire. The letter is from Pope Benedict XV. It doesn't bless a side. It names the war for what he thinks it is.
screen: `A LETTER TO THE NATIONS AT WAR.` → `THE SAME MASS, OPPOSITE TRENCHES.` → `NO SIDE BLESSED.`

segments.voice: First, the phrase. Benedict asked whether the civilized world must become a field of death, and he called the war a useless slaughter. Not glorious, not holy. Useless. Second, the plan. He didn't stop at grief. He proposed terms: that the moral force of right should take the place of the force of arms, that nations reduce their weapons together, that disputes go to arbitration instead of battle, that the seas be free, and that occupied lands be given back. Third, the answer. Governments on both sides turned it down or ignored it, and some accused him of secretly favoring the enemy. The war went on. Fourth, the other work. While the plan failed, the Vatican did what it could beside it: helping find missing soldiers, passing news between prisoners and their families, and sending relief to the hungry. In the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Notice that the line doesn't promise peacemakers success. Benedict XV didn't get his peace. What he left was a plan on paper and a name for the war: useless slaughter, from a pope who would not call it glorious.
screen: `A FIELD OF DEATH.` · `A PLAN FOR PEACE.` · `REJECTED BY BOTH SIDES.` · `PRISONERS, MISSING, HUNGRY.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind people in uniform right now, on any side of any conflict: someone young on watch at night, someone wounded, someone home who can't sleep, a family waiting by a phone. If you pray, hold them before God without asking which side they're on; if not, hold them in your attention and wish them safety and a way home.
Inutile strage. Italian for useless slaughter, the phrase remembered from Pope Benedict XV's letter calling the Great War useless and proposing terms for peace.
Your line: useless slaughter. A pope who would not bless a side. See you tomorrow.

905.title: Padre Pio (1887–1968)
905.hook: a Capuchin friar known for long confessions and the stigmata
905.howItsDone: Catholics keep Padre Pio's memorial in September; pilgrims visit San Giovanni Rotondo, Padre Pio prayer groups meet in parishes, and Catholics go to confession, often on Saturdays or before great feasts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benedict XV, who called the Great War inutile strage, a useless slaughter. Your line was useless slaughter. Today, a friar in a small town, and a very long line.

Two hands in brown fingerless gloves, resting on the edge of a confessional. In San Giovanni Rotondo, a town on a mountainside in southern Italy, people gather outside a friary church before dawn to kneel in front of those hands. Farmers, visitors from far away, people who haven't been to church in years. They're not there for a show. They want a few minutes with a bearded Capuchin friar in a brown habit. The gloves cover something he would rather not put on display. His name is Padre Pio.
screen: `TWO GLOVED HANDS.` → `A CROWD BEFORE DAWN.` → `A FRIAR IN A BROWN HABIT.`

segments.voice: Four sides of the man. First, the confessional. Padre Pio spent long hours, day after day, hearing confessions. People said he could be gentle and also blunt; tradition says he sometimes sent a person away to come back more honest. Second, the wounds. He carried marks on his hands, feet and side, like the wounds of Christ, the stigmata. That's why the gloves. Saint Paul writes to the Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body." Doctors examined him. Some were convinced, some skeptical. Third, the obedience. Church authorities investigated him more than once, and for a time they restricted his ministry, keeping him from saying Mass in public and from hearing confessions. He obeyed, and waited. The restrictions were later eased. When the Church canonized him, it honored his holiness of life; Catholics remain free to judge the wounds for themselves. Fourth, the work and the advice. He built a hospital in the town, the Home for the Relief of Suffering, and encouraged people to form prayer groups. And there is a line attributed to him that people still repeat, simple enough to fit on a fridge magnet: pray, hope, and don't worry. Three short verbs. For a friar who spent his days hearing the worst of people's lives, it is a surprisingly light thing to say.
screen: `HOURS IN THE CONFESSIONAL.` · `THE MARKS OF CHRIST.` · `INVESTIGATED, AND OBEDIENT.` · `PRAY, HOPE, DON'T WORRY.` · then, large: `I BEAR THE MARKS.`

segments.voice: Picture the crowd outside his church before dawn, and yourself somewhere in it: when your turn came, what would you want to set down? Let one honest sentence form; if you're Catholic, it may belong in confession, and if you're not, ask who that sentence is owed to. Either way, end with the friar's three words: pray, hope, don't worry.

906.title: Faustina Kowalska (1905–1938)
906.hook: a Polish sister records a message of mercy: Jesus, I trust in you
906.howItsDone: Catholics who keep this devotion pray the Divine Mercy chaplet on rosary beads, often at three in the afternoon, and the image with its signature 'Jesus, I trust in you' hangs in parish churches; the Sunday after Easter is kept as Divine Mercy Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Padre Pio, the friar with the long line outside his confessional. Your line was pray, hope, don't worry. Today, a sister who worked in kitchens and gardens and kept a diary.

A painter's studio in Vilnius. A priest has hired an artist to paint a picture to a nun's description. She comes in to check on it. Jesus in a white robe, one hand raised in blessing, the other touching his chest, where two rays stream out, one pale and one red. The nun looks at the canvas, and, by her own account in her diary, she goes away and weeps, because it isn't as beautiful as what she saw. Her name is Sister Faustina Kowalska.
screen: `A PAINTER'S STUDIO.` → `TWO RAYS, ONE PALE, ONE RED.` → `SHE WEEPS AT THE CANVAS.`

segments.voice: First, the ordinary work. She came from a poor farming family in Poland, worked as a housekeeper, then joined a congregation of sisters. There she did the plain jobs: cook, gardener, the sister at the gate. Second, the message. She wrote that Jesus spoke to her about his mercy, asked for the image to be painted, and asked that it carry a signature: Jesus, I trust in you. At her confessor's request, she wrote down what she experienced in a diary, which became a long book. Third, the chaplet. She recorded a short prayer, prayed on ordinary rosary beads, that keeps asking for mercy on us and on the whole world. It takes a few minutes. Catholics pray it at home, in hospitals, and at three in the afternoon, the hour tradition links to Jesus's death. Fourth, the old word. Divine Mercy was not a new idea. Psalm one hundred thirty-five, in the Douay-Rheims, repeats one refrain over and over: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Faustina's message sends people back to that refrain, with a name and a face attached, and asks for one thing in return: trust. Not trust that life will go smoothly. Faustina was ill for years and died young. Trust, as she wrote of it, that mercy is bigger than anything a person has done. The Church later canonized her, and her image now hangs in churches far from Poland, the rays still pale and red, the line still underneath.
screen: `A COOK AND A GARDENER.` · `A NOTEBOOK OF MERCY.` · `A CHAPLET ON ROSARY BEADS.` · `AN OLD REFRAIN.` · then, large: `HIS MERCY ENDURETH FOR EVER.`

segments.voice: If you pray, take rosary beads or use your fingers, and on each bead ask for mercy on yourself and on the whole world, in the chaplet's words or your own; the whole chaplet runs longer than this, so simply begin. If you don't pray, let one face come to mind, someone you find hard to forgive, and hold it a moment without judging it. Then rest.

907.title: Kolbe before Auschwitz
907.hook: a friar with a printing press, a magazine for Mary, and a mission to Japan
907.howItsDone: Catholics who join the Militia Immaculatae, the movement Kolbe started, consecrate themselves to Mary and pray for others, and Catholic media groups sometimes name Kolbe as an example for their work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Faustina and the Divine Mercy. Your line was jesus, I trust in you. Today, a friar who trusted enough to buy a printing press.

Ink on his fingers. A Polish Franciscan friar in round glasses bends over an old hand press, cranking out pages of a small magazine. He has very little money and a weak chest, and his own brothers are not sure about this project. The magazine is called the Knight of the Immaculata. He hands copies out, mails them, begs for paper. This path met Maximilian Kolbe at the end of his story, in a starvation cell, offering his life for another prisoner. Today goes back to the middle: the years when he was building something, loudly, with machines.
screen: `INK ON HIS FINGERS.` → `A MAGAZINE CALLED THE KNIGHT.` → `THE MIDDLE OF THE STORY.`

segments.voice: First, the knight. As a young friar in Rome, Kolbe and a few companions started a movement they called the Militia Immaculatae, the army of the Immaculate, meaning Mary. A knight, in his sense, carried no sword. He carried prayer and a promise to win people over to God through Mary, by any good means at hand. Second, the press. Back in Poland, his means at hand was paper. The magazine grew. He and his brothers built a friary near Warsaw, Niepokalanów, the city of the Immaculate, and filled it with presses and friars who ran them. Kolbe wanted the newest machines. To him, a fast press was a tool for good, the same way a pulpit was. Third, Japan. He sailed east and landed in Nagasaki with almost nothing, not even the language. Soon there was a Japanese edition of the magazine, and a small friary on a hillside outside the city. Fourth, the housetops. Jesus says in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "That which I tell you in the dark, speak ye in the light: and that which you hear in the ear, preach ye upon the housetops." Kolbe treated the newest media of his day as a housetop. The same knight who later stepped forward in Auschwitz spent his working years putting presses, paper and post to that use. Put as a question for today: can this carry something good to someone who needs it?
screen: `THE KNIGHT CARRIES NO SWORD.` · `A CITY OF PRINTING PRESSES.` · `A FRIARY IN NAGASAKI.` · `MEDIA AS A HOUSETOP.` · then, large: `PREACH YE UPON THE HOUSETOPS.`

segments.voice: Take out your phone, or just picture its screen, and notice what it usually carries: news, noise, arguments, photos, a few kind words. Think of one person who could use something good today, a friend who's struggling, a parent who's lonely, and choose what you could send: a photo, a thank-you, a line that helped you. 908.title: Edith Stein (1891–1942)
908.hook: a Jewish philosopher becomes a Carmelite nun, and is murdered at Auschwitz with her sister
908.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of St. Teresa Benedicta of the Cross in August, and she is honored as one of the patron saints of Europe; Carmelites read her writings on the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kolbe before Auschwitz, and the Militia Immaculatae: a friar with printing presses and a magazine for Mary. Your line was the knight. Today, another name tied to that same camp.

A borrowed book, read through the night. The reader is a young philosopher, brilliant, Jewish by birth, and for years she has called herself an unbeliever. She's staying at a friend's house, picks up the life of Teresa of Ávila, the Spanish Carmelite, and doesn't put it down. Tradition says that when she closed it at dawn, she said: this is the truth. Edith Stein's mother kept the Jewish faith, and her daughter's choice would cost them both a great deal. Today is her road, from the lecture hall to the convent to a train going east.
screen: `A BOOK READ THROUGH THE NIGHT.` → `THIS IS THE TRUTH.` → `LECTURE HALL, CONVENT, TRAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the thinker. She studied philosophy in Germany and worked closely with Edmund Husserl, whose way of thinking, called phenomenology, looks carefully at experience itself. Her doctoral work was on empathy, how one person can truly feel into another's life. Second, the convert. After that night with Teresa, she asked for baptism and was received into the Catholic Church. She taught and lectured, until the Nazi laws pushed Jewish teachers out of their posts. Third, the Carmelite. She entered Carmel in Cologne and took a new name: Teresa Benedicta of the Cross. Teresa, after the book. Benedicta, blessed. And of the cross, because she believed she was being drawn into Christ's suffering, alongside her own people's. Saint Paul writes in Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Her sisters moved her to a Carmel in the Netherlands for safety. Fourth, the train. In the Netherlands, she and her sister Rosa, also a Catholic convert, were arrested and sent to Auschwitz, where they were murdered. They were killed because they were born Jewish. The Church honors her as a saint and a martyr. Some Jewish voices have asked that her story never blur that fact, and that her death be remembered with the death of her people. Both things are true of her.
screen: `THE PHILOSOPHER OF EMPATHY.` · `BAPTIZED AFTER ONE BOOK.` · `TERESA BENEDICTA OF THE CROSS.` · `KILLED BECAUSE SHE WAS BORN JEWISH.` · then, large: `SAVE IN THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: Let Edith and Rosa stand a moment in your mind, two sisters on one train, then widen it: the families on that train and the others, with names and kitchens and jokes and recipes. You don't need to imagine the horror; just hold the people. If you pray, pray for them in your own words; if not, keep the silence for them.

909.title: The Holocaust, honestly
909.hook: Catholics were among the rescuers, the bystanders and the perpetrators, and the Church's document We Remember asked for repentance
909.howItsDone: Some Catholic parishes and schools mark Holocaust Remembrance Day with prayer, survivor testimony and joint services with Jewish communities, and the Church's documents on Catholic-Jewish relations are studied in seminaries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Edith Stein, Teresa Benedicta of the Cross, killed with her sister because they were born Jewish. Your line was her religious name. Today we stay with the whole of it. Go gently.

A question from the first family in Genesis. Cain has killed his brother, and God asks him where Abel is. Cain answers with a question of his own, in the Douay-Rheims: "am I my brother's keeper?" During the Holocaust, when Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered Europe's Jews, that question was answered town by town, by all kinds of people. Baptized Catholics were among the people who answered it. Some answered yes, at the cost of their lives. Some looked away. And some were the killers. Today is not a saint's story. It's an honest one.
screen: `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?` → `ANSWERED TOWN BY TOWN.` → `NOT A SAINT'S STORY.`

segments.voice: Four honest things. First, the rescuers. Priests, sisters, farmers and families hid Jewish neighbors in convents, attics and barns, forged papers, and carried children to safety. Some were caught and killed for it. In a few days we'll meet one of them by name. Second, the bystanders. Others did nothing. They saw neighbors taken away and stayed quiet, out of fear, or indifference, or a habit of thinking of Jews as other. Third, the perpetrators. Some who carried out the murders had been baptized, sat in pews, and took communion. Nothing in their faith stopped them. Fourth, the reckoning. The Vatican later published a document called We Remember: A Reflection on the Shoah. Shoah is the Hebrew word for catastrophe, a word Jewish people use for the Holocaust. The document says, in its own words, that the Church deeply regrets the failures of her sons and daughters in that time, and calls that an act of repentance. It also names a long history of anti-Jewish teaching and feeling among Christians, and says that it left some Christians less ready to resist. Some Jewish readers welcomed the document; some said it did not go far enough, especially on the Church's leaders in those years. Both reactions are part of the record. The document's title is a promise: to remember, so that the seeds of anti-Judaism and antisemitism are never again allowed to take root.
screen: `THE RESCUERS.` · `THE BYSTANDERS.` · `THE PERPETRATORS.` · `WE REMEMBER: A CALL TO REPENT.` · then, large: `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?`

segments.voice: Let the word survivor sit with you: a real person who lived through it, with a name, a face, and a life afterward. If you've heard one survivor's story, in a book, a talk, a recording, or from a relative, bring it back now and stay with that one person; if not, simply hold the people who lived it. If you pray, pray for them and for the dead.

910.title: Franz Jägerstätter (1907–1943)
910.hook: an Austrian farmer refuses to fight for Hitler and is executed
910.howItsDone: Catholics honor Blessed Franz Jägerstätter as a martyr of conscience; his village parish and Catholic peace groups keep his memory with prayer and readings from his prison letters.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Holocaust, told honestly: rescuers, bystanders and killers. Your line was we remember. Today, one man who refused to go along.

A village in the Austrian hills. When Austria is joined to Hitler's Germany, the people vote on it, and the result in his village is yes. One farmer votes no. He's not a priest or a professor. Franz Jägerstätter farms, with a wife named Franziska and young daughters. In the war years he also becomes the sacristan at the parish church, ringing the bell and setting out the vessels for Mass. Then a call-up letter orders him to report for duty. He reports, and he tells them he will not fight.
screen: `ONE VOTE AGAINST.` → `A FARMER AND A SACRISTAN.` → `I WILL NOT FIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the conscience. Franz had thought it through, in prayer and on paper. He believed the Nazi cause was evil, and that fighting for it would be a sin he could not commit. Second, the advice. He was not cheered on. His parish priest and his bishop urged him to serve, for the sake of his family, telling him the responsibility belonged to those who gave the orders. People in the village thought he was throwing his life away. He listened to them with respect, and still said no. Third, the prison. He was arrested, tried and sentenced to death. In his cell he wrote letters to Franziska, full of love for her and the girls, and notes on why he could not do what he was told. Franziska stood by him. Fourth, the scaffold. He was executed, and for years some in his village and his Church treated him as a man who had abandoned his family. Later, the Church beatified him as a martyr, with Franziska still living to see it. The apostles told the authorities in Acts, in the Douay-Rheims: "We ought to obey God, rather than men." Franz took that line seriously, even against the advice of those he trusted. This week ran from a pope who called a war a useless slaughter, through a friar's confessional, a sister's diary, Kolbe's presses, Edith Stein and the hard record of the Holocaust, to a farmer who said no.

segments.voice: Ask yourself quietly where you're going along with something you know isn't right: a joke at someone's expense, a shortcut at work, a silence when something should be said. Don't pick the biggest thing; pick a small one, the size of one vote in one village, and picture what saying no would look like. If you pray, ask for courage.
